title: L4 vs L7 Load Balancing & Algorithms
subtitle: TLS termination, health checks, Least-Conn & PEWMA routing
overview: Load balancers decouple clients from volatile backend fleets. Layer 4 (Transport) forwards TCP packets at wire speed via DSR/NAT without decrypting TLS; Layer 7 (Application) terminates TLS, inspects HTTP paths/headers, and chooses backends dynamically using Least-Connections or latency-aware PEWMA.
firstPrinciplesStory: You add 8 shiny new backend pods behind a basic L4 Load Balancer during a traffic spike, expecting load to drop by 3x. Instead, the original 4 pods melt at 98% CPU while your 8 new pods sit completely idle! Why? Because HTTP/2 and gRPC multiplex hundreds of requests over ONE long-lived TCP socket—and L4 balances connections, not requests. Understanding where L4 stops and L7 takes over saves you from mysterious horizontal-scaling failures.

adaptiveLenses.intuition: An L4 balancer is an expressway tollbooth waving entire sealed trucks (TCP connections) into lanes without looking inside; an L7 proxy opens each truck, reads individual package labels (HTTP routes/RPCs), and steers packages away from slow loading docks.
adaptiveLenses.mechanics: Production ingress pairs L4 ECMP/Maglev (routing millions of packets/sec via 5-tuple hash) in front of L7 Envoy proxies. Envoy terminates TLS 1.3, tracks active in-flight streams and exponentially smoothed latency (PEWMA), and ejects gray-failing backends via passive outlier detection.
adaptiveLenses.staffTradeoffs: Round Robin works poorly when request cost varies wildly (e.g., 2ms cache check vs 400ms PDF export) or during GC pauses. Power-of-Two-Choices + PEWMA balances tail latency cleanly without O(N) global state contention, while strict retry budgets (<20%) prevent retry storms.

ddiaAnchors.whyItMatters: A single slow backend pod inflates tail latency across callers unless latency-aware load balancers steer around it.

pragmaticTips.tip: Keep TLS termination, auth verification, and canary routing in an orthogonal L7 gateway layer rather than copy-pasting middleware across 20 services.
pragmaticTips.application: Upgrade TLS ciphers or swap routing weights once at Envoy without redeploying backend business pods.

keyTakeaways: L4 load balancers handle millions of packets/sec via 5-tuple hashing; L7 proxies inspect HTTP routes, JWTs, and gRPC frames.
Real production architectures stack L4 (Anycast/ECMP VIP) in front of L7 Envoy/NGINX proxy fleets.
Latency-aware routing (Least Connections + PEWMA) outperforms static Round Robin when requests have uneven compute cost.

nodes.label: Client Fleet
nodes.summary: External API callers maintaining multiplexed TLS connections.
failureModes: HTTP/2 long-lived TCP pinning starves new backend pods unless L7 re-balances per stream

nodes.label: L4 Maglev / NLB
nodes.summary: Stateless packet-level balancer distributing raw TCP flows across L7 proxy nodes.
whenToUse: First ingress tier handling multi-million PPS DDoS/TLS scale
failureModes: Cannot route on URL path or HTTP headers

nodes.label: L7 Envoy Proxy
nodes.summary: Terminates TLS, enforces path routing, tracks active in-flight requests and EWMA backend latency.
whenToUse: Path-based microservice routing, canary traffic splitting, gRPC multiplexing
failureModes: CPU bottleneck from TLS handshakes if session tickets aren't shared

nodes.label: App Pod A
failureModes: GC pauses or thread pool saturation

nodes.label: App Pod B (Slow)
nodes.summary: Degraded replica experiencing elevated GC/CPU contention.
whenToUse: Demonstrates why static Round Robin hurts tail latency
failureModes: Gray failure: returns 200 OK slowly, bypassing naive ping checks

nodes.label: App Pod C
nodes.summary: Under-utilized healthy replica selected by PEWMA / Power-of-2-Choices.
failureModes: Pod startup cold JIT without warmup ramp

predictPrompt.prompt: Why does Pod B's `/health` endpoint still returning `200 OK` fail to protect users under static Round Robin?
predictPrompt.hint: Think about what a simple liveness ping measures vs actual heavy business RPC latency.
predictPrompt.reveal: A shallow `/health` check returns `200 OK` quickly even when database pools or GC pauses stall real `/checkout` RPCs at 140ms+ (a gray failure). Latency-aware PEWMA + passive error tracking catches this immediately.

steps.inspectorNote: Total proxy + compute latency stays under 10ms while Pod B would have caused a 140ms p99 spike.

chaosScenarios.title: Passive Health Check & Outlier Ejection
chaosScenarios.triggerSummary: App Pod B starts returning consecutive 502/timeouts under memory pressure.
chaosScenarios.mitigationSummary: Envoy passive outlier detection ejects Pod B for 30s after 5 consecutive 5xx errors and drains existing requests to Pod A/C.

steps.info: 5 consecutive 503/timeout failures detected on App Pod B
steps.inspectorNote: Passive health checks react within milliseconds of real traffic errors, far faster than 10s periodic HTTP probes.

steps.info: Idempotent GET safely retried on Pod A -> 200 OK (8 ms)
steps.inspectorNote: With retry budgets capped (e.g. 20% max retries), Pod A absorbs the request cleanly without retry amplification.
